subject: ela
intro: Each item gives you a transcript of what a speaker actually said. Read it as if you were listening to the speech, report, or debate turn. Then analyze the spoken argument: match a claim to the support behind it, tell a reason apart from evidence, or decide which claim the speaker leaves unsupported. The speaker uses both strong support and weak support, so weigh how good each piece of support really is.

items.prompt:
Transcript of a student's speech to the school board: 'I am asking the board to add a late bus at 5:00. Right now the only bus leaves at 3:15, and that creates a real problem. Last fall our school counted students who stay for clubs and sports, and 142 students were still in the building after 3:15 with no way home. Many of them call a parent to leave work early. A 5:00 bus would also help students stay safe, because walking home in the dark along Route 9, where there is no sidewalk, is dangerous. Trust me, everyone I know agrees a late bus is just the right thing to do. Please vote yes.'

The speaker makes two claims: (1) a late bus is needed, and (2) it would help students stay safe. Which claim does the speaker support with evidence, and which is supported only by opinion?
items.answer: The need for a late bus is supported with evidence (the count of 142 students stranded after 3:15), while the safety claim is backed by a real reason (no sidewalk on Route 9 in the dark) plus the line 'everyone I know agrees,' which is only opinion, not proof.

steps: Find each claim and look for the support attached to it.
For the 'need' claim, the speaker cites a concrete count: 142 students were stranded after the 3:15 bus. That is evidence.
For the safety claim, the speaker gives a reason (no sidewalk on Route 9 in the dark), but then adds 'everyone I know agrees,' which is opinion stated as if it settled the matter.
So the need claim rests on evidence, while the persuasive 'everyone agrees' line is opinion, not proof that the bus is needed or safe.

items.prompt:
Transcript of an oral report on recycling: 'Our town should switch to a single recycling bin instead of three sorting bins. First, single-bin recycling raises how much people recycle. When the city of Maple Grove switched last year, the amount collected went up 30 percent in six months, according to their public works report. Second, single bins save money. Trucks only have to make one stop instead of three, which the report says cut collection costs by a fifth. Finally, single bins are simply better, and anyone who cares about the planet can see that. So I urge the town council to make the change this spring.'

The speaker makes three claims. Which claim is left unsupported, resting on opinion rather than reasons or evidence?
items.answer: The third claim, that single bins are 'simply better' and 'anyone who cares about the planet can see that,' is unsupported. It offers no reason or evidence, only an opinion and a loaded appeal.

steps: Check each claim for the support behind it.
Claim one (recycling rises) is backed by evidence: Maple Grove's amount went up 30 percent, from a public works report.
Claim two (saves money) is backed by a reason and a figure: one stop instead of three cut costs by a fifth.
Claim three says single bins are 'simply better' and that caring people 'can see that.' No reason or evidence is given, so this claim is unsupported and leans on opinion and loaded wording.

items.prompt:
Transcript of a debate turn on homework: 'I argue that middle schools should cap homework at one hour a night. Here is why. Studies of sixth graders found that beyond one hour, test scores stop improving, so extra homework past that point does not help learning. That is the reason a cap makes sense. Now, what is my proof? A 2019 study at our regional university tracked 600 students and found their grades were the same whether they did one hour or three hours of homework. Some people will say students just need to work harder, but the data shows more hours did not raise grades. A one-hour cap respects students' time without hurting their learning.'

In this argument, which part is the reason and which part is the evidence the speaker gives for capping homework?
items.answer: The reason is that homework past one hour does not improve learning. The evidence is the 2019 university study of 600 students whose grades were the same after one hour or three hours of homework.

steps: A reason is the logic for why the claim is true; evidence is the concrete proof.
The speaker states the reason: beyond one hour, extra homework 'does not help learning.' That is the why.
The speaker then offers proof: the 2019 study of 600 students whose grades did not change with more hours. That is the concrete evidence.
So the reason explains why a cap makes sense, and the study is the evidence that backs the reason.

items.prompt:
Transcript of a presentation to the principal: 'We need a longer lunch period. Right now lunch is 22 minutes. By the time students get through the line and sit down, they have about 10 minutes to eat. The school nurse reported that visits for stomachaches rose this year, and she believes rushed eating is one cause. A longer lunch would also make the cafeteria less crowded if we split it into two waves. Honestly, short lunch is the worst thing about this school, and I think everybody is miserable about it. Please give us 30 minutes.'

The speaker claims students do not have enough time to eat. Which statement from the speech is the evidence for that claim, not just an opinion?
items.answer: The evidence is that lunch is 22 minutes and, after the line, students have about 10 minutes to actually eat. The line 'everybody is miserable about it' is opinion, not evidence.

steps: The claim is that students lack enough time to eat.
Look for a concrete detail that proves it: the 22-minute period and the roughly 10 minutes left to eat after the line are specific facts.
'Everybody is miserable' and 'the worst thing about this school' are feelings and opinions, not measured evidence.
So the timing details are the evidence; the misery line is an emotional appeal.

items.prompt:
Transcript of a science fair presentation: 'My project shows that plants grow taller with music. I played classical music to one set of bean plants for two weeks and kept another set in silence. The music plants grew an average of 14 centimeters, and the silent plants grew 11 centimeters. So music clearly makes plants grow. Plants must enjoy music the same way people do, and that is obviously why they grew more. My results prove that every gardener should play music to their plants.'

The speaker claims plants grow taller with music. Which claim in this speech is stated without any real support?
items.answer: The claim that 'plants must enjoy music the same way people do,' offered as the reason for the growth, is stated with no support. It is a guess presented as fact, not backed by the experiment.

steps: The growth claim has some evidence: the 14 cm versus 11 cm measurement from the speaker's own test.
But the speaker also claims plants 'enjoy music the same way people do' and that this is 'obviously why they grew.'
Nothing in the experiment measured enjoyment, so that explanation has no support and is asserted as if obvious.
Therefore the 'plants enjoy music' claim is the unsupported one, even though it sounds like a tidy explanation.

items.prompt:
Transcript of a club leader's pitch: 'The robotics club needs the larger room, Room 214. We have grown from 8 members to 25 members this year, our sign-in sheets show it. With 25 students, our current room only has 16 chairs, so almost ten kids sit on the floor every meeting. Room 214 has 30 seats and wide tables for building. The art club currently uses 214, but they only meet twice a month, while we meet every week. A bigger, busier club should get the bigger room. Please approve the switch.'

What specific evidence does the speaker give to support the claim that the robotics club has outgrown its current room?
items.answer: The speaker shows the club grew from 8 to 25 members (confirmed by sign-in sheets) while the current room has only 16 chairs, leaving about ten students sitting on the floor. That size-versus-seats gap is the evidence.

steps: The claim is that the club has outgrown its room.
Look for concrete numbers tied to that claim: membership rose from 8 to 25, backed by sign-in sheets.
The current room has only 16 chairs, so roughly ten students sit on the floor each week.

The mismatch between 25 members and 16 chairs is the evidence that the club has outgrown the space. The point that art club meets less often supports a different claim (who deserves 214), not the outgrowing claim.

items.prompt:
Transcript of a speech urging a phone ban: 'Phones should be banned during class. When a school in our district banned phones, teachers reported far fewer interruptions, and quiz averages rose by six points over the semester. That is strong proof a ban helps focus. Also, phones are just bad for kids, plain and simple. Everyone knows screens are ruining this generation. With a ban, students would finally pay attention. I hope our school follows the same path.'

The speaker makes two claims to support a ban. Which claim is supported by evidence, and which is only a sweeping generalization?
items.answer: The claim that a ban improves focus is supported by evidence (the district school's six-point rise in quiz averages and fewer interruptions). The claim that 'phones are just bad for kids' and 'screens are ruining this generation' is a sweeping generalization with no proof.

steps: Separate the two claims and check each for support.
The focus claim is backed by results from a real school: fewer interruptions and a six-point rise in quiz averages. That is evidence.
The 'phones are just bad' and 'screens are ruining this generation' lines name no facts and apply to everyone at once.
A statement that sweeping with no proof is a generalization, so it is the unsupported claim.

items.prompt:
Transcript of an oral report on the school garden: 'Our school garden should be expanded. The garden already feeds people: last year it grew 300 pounds of vegetables, which the cafeteria used in salads, according to our garden log. Expanding it would let us grow even more. A bigger garden would also teach science, since students measure plant growth and test soil there, and our science teacher confirmed she uses it in three lessons. Plus, gardens just make everybody happy, and a happy school is a better school. Let us double the garden's size next year.'

The speaker gives several reasons to expand the garden. Which reason does the speaker fail to back up with any evidence?
items.answer: The reason that 'gardens just make everybody happy, and a happy school is a better school' is not backed up. No evidence is given for the happiness claim; it is an opinion presented as fact.

steps: List the reasons and check which have evidence.
The food reason has evidence: 300 pounds of vegetables from the garden log.
The science reason has evidence: the science teacher confirmed she uses the garden in three lessons.
The happiness reason ('gardens just make everybody happy') has no measurement or source, so it is the reason left without support.

items.prompt:
Transcript of a debate turn on dress codes: 'The dress code should be relaxed. My main point is that strict codes do not improve behavior, they just create conflict. Consider the evidence: a 2021 survey of 12 middle schools found no link between strict dress codes and fewer behavior problems. The schools with strict codes had the same rate of incidents as the schools without them. That survey is the proof behind my point. Some say codes teach professionalism, but the survey shows codes did not change conduct at all. A relaxed code respects students and avoids needless arguments.'

Identify the speaker's reason and the evidence in this argument about dress codes.
items.answer: The reason is that strict dress codes do not improve behavior and only create conflict. The evidence is the 2021 survey of 12 middle schools that found no link between strict codes and fewer behavior problems.

steps: The reason is the logic the speaker gives: strict codes do not improve behavior, they cause conflict.
The evidence is the concrete data: the 2021 survey of 12 schools showing the same incident rate with or without strict codes.
The survey is the proof, and the 'do not improve behavior' statement is the reasoning it supports.
So the reason explains the position and the survey is the evidence behind it.

items.prompt:
Transcript of a presentation on bottled water: 'Our school should remove the bottled water machines and add more water fountains. First, fountains cost less over time. The school spends about $4,000 a year on bottled water, the office told me, while a fountain costs $1,200 once. Second, fountains cut down on plastic waste, and our custodian counted over 200 empty bottles in the trash each week. Third, bottled water is honestly a scam by big companies who just want our money, and we should not let them win. Let us make the switch and install three new fountains.'

The speaker offers three reasons. Two are supported and one is not. Which reason is unsupported, and what makes it weak?
items.answer: The third reason, that bottled water is 'a scam by big companies' who 'want our money,' is unsupported. It uses loaded, biased wording and gives no facts, unlike the cost and waste reasons that come with numbers.

steps: Check each reason for evidence.
Reason one (cost) has figures: $4,000 a year versus a $1,200 fountain, from the office.
Reason two (waste) has a count: over 200 empty bottles each week, from the custodian.
Reason three calls bottled water 'a scam' and accuses companies of greed, with no facts. That loaded wording is an appeal, not evidence, so it is the unsupported reason.

items.prompt:
Transcript of a speech about a new crosswalk: 'We need a crosswalk on Pine Street by the school. I have two main claims. First, the street is dangerous to cross. The city traffic study counted 80 cars an hour during morning drop-off, and there is no marked crossing for three blocks. Second, students already cross there anyway. I watched for one week and saw students dart across Pine Street 40 to 50 times each morning. A painted crosswalk and a sign would slow drivers and give students a safe place to cross. The city should add one before someone gets hurt.'

Match the speaker's claim that students already cross Pine Street to the specific evidence given for it.
items.answer: The evidence for the claim that students already cross there is the speaker's week-long observation of students darting across Pine Street 40 to 50 times each morning. The 80-cars-per-hour figure supports the different claim that the street is dangerous.

steps: Find the claim in question: students already cross Pine Street.
Look for the support tied to that exact claim, not a different one.
The speaker's own week of watching, counting 40 to 50 crossings each morning, is the evidence that students already cross.
The 80-cars-per-hour count proves danger, a separate claim, so it is not the match for this claim.

items.prompt:
Transcript of an oral report on sleep: 'Middle schools should start later, around 8:30 instead of 7:30. Doctors say sixth graders need about nine hours of sleep, but with a 7:30 start most get only seven. That gap is the core reason for my proposal. As for proof, a district that moved its start time to 8:30 reported that tardiness dropped by 25 percent and the school nurse saw fewer students falling asleep in class, according to their year-end report. Later start times also feel kinder, and a kind school is a good school. We should follow this plan and protect students' health.'

The speaker mixes solid support with a weak line. Which statement is offered as proof but is actually just an opinion?
items.answer: The line 'later start times also feel kinder, and a kind school is a good school' is an opinion, not proof. The real evidence is the district report showing tardiness dropped 25 percent and fewer students fell asleep in class.

steps: Separate the genuine evidence from the opinion.
The district report (tardiness down 25 percent, fewer students asleep in class) is concrete evidence from a source.
The 'feels kinder' and 'a kind school is a good school' line states a feeling with no facts behind it.
So the kindness line is opinion dressed up as support, while the district report is the actual proof.

items.prompt:
Transcript of a debate turn on field trips: 'My side argues for more field trips. Field trips boost learning, and here is the proof: after our class visited the science museum, our unit test average rose from 78 to 88, the teacher shared the scores. Field trips also build teamwork, since students solve challenges together at sites like the ropes course, and our advisor noted stronger group projects afterward. My opponent says trips waste class time, but the higher test scores show the time was well spent. Clearly, the more trips the better, no matter the cost. Let us schedule at least four trips this year.'

The speaker claims 'the more trips the better, no matter the cost.' Why is this final claim weak, even though earlier claims were supported?
items.answer: The final claim is weak because the speaker gives no evidence that more trips, regardless of cost, keep helping. The earlier evidence (test scores rising 78 to 88) supports trips in general, not the sweeping 'no matter the cost' conclusion, which overreaches the proof.

steps: Earlier claims were supported: the museum trip evidence (78 to 88) and the advisor's note on teamwork.
The final claim jumps to 'the more trips the better, no matter the cost.'
No evidence shows that adding many trips, or ignoring cost, still helps. The data was about one trip's effect.
Because the conclusion stretches far beyond what the evidence proves, it is a weak, unsupported overgeneralization.

items.prompt:
Transcript of a speech to start a chess club: 'We should start a chess club. There is clear interest: I posted a sign-up sheet and 34 students signed it in two days. Chess also helps thinking skills, and a study cited by our math teacher found students who played chess weekly improved their problem-solving scores. We already have a teacher willing to sponsor it, Ms. Lee said yes. And honestly, chess is just the smartest game there is, way better than anything else, so of course we should have a club. Please approve our new club.'

The speaker gives several supported claims and one unsupported one. Which claim is supported only by the speaker's personal opinion?
items.answer: The claim that 'chess is just the smartest game there is, way better than anything else' is supported only by the speaker's opinion. No evidence backs it, unlike the sign-up count, the study, and the sponsor.

steps: Check each claim for evidence.
Interest is supported: 34 students signed up in two days.
Thinking skills are supported: a study cited by the math teacher. The sponsor is confirmed: Ms. Lee said yes.
The claim that chess is 'the smartest game there is, way better than anything else' has no proof and is a personal opinion, so it is the unsupported one.

items.prompt:
Transcript of an oral report on water bottles being banned at the gym: 'I argue the gym should keep allowing reusable water bottles. First, students need water during exercise. Our PE teacher said classes now run 50 minutes of activity, and the school nurse warned that students without water risk getting dizzy or overheated. That is a real safety reason. Second, banning bottles would not even fix the spill problem the principal mentioned, because the gym's records show only two spills all year, hardly a crisis. People against bottles say they cause messes, but two spills in a year is not a mess problem. Reusable bottles keep students safe, so they should stay.'

The speaker responds to the claim that bottles cause messes. What evidence does the speaker give to weaken that opposing claim?
items.answer: The speaker cites the gym's records showing only two spills all year, which is too few to count as a real mess problem. That record is the evidence used to weaken the opposing claim.

steps: The opposing claim is that bottles cause messes.
Find the speaker's evidence against it: the gym's records show only two spills in the entire year.
Two spills a year is presented as far too few to be a 'mess problem,' which directly weakens the opposing claim.
The safety points (50 minutes of activity, risk of dizziness) support a different claim, that students need water, not the spill rebuttal.
